title: Latency-slotted prefetch and tool-commit proposal
body:
Summary:

This is an exploratory PRD sketch for a latency-focused streaming pattern were calling "latency-slotted prefetch" paired with a small set of tool-commit primitives. The goal: give client SDKs a predictable low-latency fast-path for common interactive flows while enabling safe, resumable tool execution and structured, schema-backed commit frames.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Many customers build interactive features (chat assistants, code copilots, search summarizers) that require ultra-low median latency for the first few tokens while still invoking heavyweight tool calls (search, DB reads, code execution).
- Current approaches force a trade-off: either wait synchronously for tool results (higher P50/P95) or optimistic prefetch that sometimes wastes work and produces confusing outputs when tool results contradict generation.
- SDK ergonomics for consumers are often complex: handling partial results, reconciling later commits, and ensuring idempotency for tool calls is error-prone.

Objectives (what success looks like):
1) Reduce median time-to-first-meaningful-token by ~20-40% for interactive flows where the model may need tool outputs for fidelity but can safely begin an initial fast-path reply.
2) Provide a compact, well-documented commit primitive that carries structured changes (schema, confidence, trace id) so clients can reconcile and apply authoritative tool results without full conversation replay.
3) Keep server-side scheduling and cost predictable (bounded prefetch work per request) and expose telemetry to quantify wasted prefetch and commit mismatches.

Non-goals:
- This is not a new general-purpose tool orchestration language. Its an ergonomic surface for interactive SDKs to get better latency economics and clearer reconciliation primitives.
- Not addressing long-running workflows (minutes+). Focus is interactive < 5s end-to-end.

Key concepts / definitions:
- Slot: a short latency budget bucket (e.g., 50ms, 150ms, 400ms) representing a stage in an incremental response. Each slot has a prefetch budget measured in token-equivalents and optional tool-run budget.
- Fast-path generation: emission of initial tokens that can be produced without authoritative tool outputs; uses cached knowledge, embeddings, and lightweight context.
- Prefetch: server-side speculative tool invocation triggered by request heuristics and historical patterns (e.g., users often call search for this prompt type). Prefetches consume the slots budget and are bounded to avoid runaway cost.
- Commit frame: a compact structured message produced when a tool returns authoritative output or when the server determines a finalization point. Commit frames carry a schema identifier, delta payload, confidence, and a deterministic id for idempotency.
- Tool-lane: a policy that maps tools to commit semantics: transient (best-effort), authoritative (single-source-of-truth), or advisory (helper info for scoring).

High-level flow (server + SDK):
1) Client opens a streaming call with explicit preferences: slot-profile (fast, balanced, accurate) and tool-policies (allow-prefetch: true/false).
2) Server immediately returns a fast-path partial stream (slot 0) with small tokens while concurrently scheduling bounded prefetches (search, DB lookups) under slot 1/2 budgets.
3) If prefetch completes within allotted slot, server emits a commit frame followed by an updated generation span that integrates tool facts (either as replacement tokens or delta patches).
4) If prefetch misses the slot, server either (a) emit a lightweight advisory commit (partial) or (b) continue with the fast-path and mark the later authoritative commit for application when it arrives (client-visible as commit frames).
5) SDK exposes a small commit-reconcile API so clients can apply commits in place or buffer them for user acknowledgement.

API surface (sketch):
- POST /v1/generate-stream (request JSON):
  - prompt, session_id, slot_profile: "fast|balanced|accurate", tool_policy_overrides: {tool_name: "disabled|advisory|authoritative"}, resume_token (optional)
  - preferences: {max_prefetch_tokens: 64, prefetch_timeout_ms: 200}
- Stream frames (server->client):
  - frame_type: "partial_tokens", payload: text fragment, slot_index: 0
  - frame_type: "advisory_commit", payload: {schema, small-delta}, confidence, slot_index
  - frame_type: "authoritative_commit", payload: {schema, delta, id}, apply_mode: "replace|patch|append", trace_id
  - frame_type: "prefetch_stats", payload: {tools_invoked, time_ms, wasted_tokens} (telemetry)

Commit semantics examples:
- Authoritative commit (search): schema: "search-1", delta: top result summary, apply_mode: "replace" -> server instructs client to replace the last span of tokens between markers with the high-fidelity summary.
- Advisory commit (spell-check): schema: "advice-1", delta: suggestions, apply_mode: "append" -> client can show suggestions inline but not replace text automatically.

SDK ergonomics (proposed minimal surface):
- generateStream(req, {onPartial, onCommit, onTelemetry}) returns a handle with methods: cancel(), awaitApplied(commitId)
- Reconcile helpers: applyCommitInPlace(textBuffer, commitFrame) -> returns newBuffer and conflict flag
- Automatic safe-apply modes: "autoroll" (apply authoritative commits automatically) and "manual" (emit UI event and surface commit for user accept)
- Retry / idempotency: commit frames include deterministic ids and server maintains a short-lived commit cache for de-duplication. SDK exposes commitSeen(commitId) so offline clients can dedupe.

Observability / telemetry requirements:
- Per-request: slot_profile, slots_used, prefetch_tool_list, commit_counts (authoritative/advisory), wasted_prefetch_tokens, time-to-first-token, time-to-commit
- Per-tool: avg latency, commit match rate (how often prefetch result matched final authoritative result), average downstream token delta size
- Alerts: high wasted_prefetch_token ratio (>15% over 1h), commit-application errors (client rejects >1% of authoritative commits in canary)

Server-side scheduling / cost controls:
- Prefetch budget: max_prefetch_tokens per-slot enforced at admission. Each tool has a token-cost estimate to convert to same unit.
- Backpressure: when system is overloaded or user disables prefetch, server drops speculative work and marks fast-path as "no-prefetch".
- Fallbacks: if commit conflicts with client-side edits (e.g., user typed while prefetch was running), server emits a conflict commit with explicit merge hints (offsets, edit deltas).

Structured output and format stability:
- Commit frames carry schema ids and a compatibility version. We will version schemas (search-1, search-2) and publish a light schema registry.
- Commit frames should be small (prefer JSON-LD-like payloads for semantics) and optionally include a base64-encoded compact patch for binary blobs.

Security and consistency considerations:
- Authoritative commits that change user-visible content must be cryptographically traceable (trace_id, signer for enterprise Private deployments).
- Tool execution may involve customer data; commits must respect access control and data residency rules.

Rollout plan and experiments:
1) Internal experiment: integrate latency-slotted prefetch into a controlled subset of Hosted API traffic (internal dev teams) using slot_profile=fast. Measure TTF token, commit match rate, wasted prefetch tokens.
2) Canary: allow select customers (opt-in) to enable slot_profile=fast. Track UX regressions, commit acceptance rates, and support tickets.
3) Gradual enablement: if match rate > 80% and wasted tokens < 10% and no user-facing regressions, advertise fast-profile as recommended for mobile clients.

Migration and compatibility notes:
- Existing streaming clients that ignore frame types will still receive partial_tokens frames and can continue to operate; commit frames are additive.
- For older SDKs, server will include an explicit compatibility header explaining commit framing so clients can opt-out automatically.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is the optimal slot split (50/150/400ms) across model families (small/medium/large)? Need experiments.
- Prefetch cost model: how to estimate token-equivalents for non-token costs (DB read, RPCs)?
- UX patterns: should authoritative commits be auto-applied for conversational assistants or always require user confirmation? (customer-configurable?)
- Schema registry service: lightweight implementation plan and enterprise on-prem sync strategy.
- Billing model: do we bill speculative prefetch tool cost when prefetch is wasted? (proposal: bill on execution, but offer a discounted speculative rate for canary customers).

Notes to self / next steps:
- Sync with runtime team (Jordan) about prefetch admission control knobs (quota-by-customer, per-request caps).
- Prototype SDK add-on with 3 callbacks and commit reconciler (Samir assigned).
- Add synthetic workload test in perf harness to measure commit latency and wasted-prefetch at scale.
- Draft confluence page that lists schema primitives for commit frames (Marda to own).

Appendix: quick mockup of minimal stream frame sequence (text):
- [slot 0 partial_tokens] "Sure — I can help summarize that."
- [slot 1 advisory_commit schema=search-1 confidence=0.42] {"summary_hint":"Top result: Redwood platform overview"}
- [slot 2 authoritative_commit schema=search-1 id=commit-ABC apply_mode=replace] {"summary":"Redwood Inference is a platform for LLM inference with hosted, dedicated, and private deployments..."}

This draft is intentionally exploratory; want feedback on the commit frame shape, slot-profile names, and SDK surface minimality.

-- Avery
